subject: Conceptual issues - 3D sampling of mistletoes in forests

messages.author: 9749dd0ac384013e
messages.subject: Conceptual issues - 3D sampling of mistletoes in forests
parts:
I want to use distance methods to sample mistletoes in forests in central Victoria, Australia. I have a number of conceptual questions - Rather than sampling a planar area, I'm actually sampling a 3 dimension space - how do i deal with mistletoes growing directly overhead? 
If i project every mistletoe occurrence onto a horizontal plane for the purposes of calculating distance, then a mistletoe growing at 35 metres above my head has a distance of 0 metres, with an assumed detection rate of 100% , which is not practically achievable. If I use the actual distance, then I will need to use actual distance for every other mistletoe as well - my survey 'area' is then a volume, in the shape of a half cylinder, but truncated above at the limit of the canopy height.
This might also breach the random positioning of transect assumption - mistletoes are actually more likely to occur at the edge of the canopy than close to the ground, so every transect I do will be somewhat biased in terms of its positioning.

I imagine I'm not unique in this  - surveying for birds in forests, arboreal mammals, butterfies etc must have run into similar issues. Has anyone solved this issue?

gm

parts:
Gregg

This subject came up just two weeks ago on the list. 

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/6yS2xi9kx1A

There are two bits of reading on the subject.  Section 9.5 of the Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications book by Buckland et al. (2015) and Section 11.1 of Advanced Distance Sampling (Buckland et al. (2004)) address the subject of distance sampling in three dimensions.  Theory and equations are presented for this situation.  The challenge is to estimate the distribution of mistletoe with respect to transects in the vertical dimension; this is usually assumed uniform for the two-dimensional case because transects can be placed randomly with respect to animal locations in the 2D plane; this is not possible in the vertical dimension.

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Conceptual issues - 3D sampling of mistletoes in forests
parts:
Hi Gregg, list,

To add to Eric's thoughts, doing it in 3D is much harder in practice - it's not a coincidence that people simplçy haven't really done it in practice. Therefore, I would possibly still project distances to the ground. Naturally, given that your object of interests might be 30 m up (and hence missedeven if on the line), you should consider a mark recapture distance sampling (MRDS) approach to estimate g0 (i.e. the probability of detection on the line).

You have the luxury of dealing with objects that move relatively slowly (MRDS methods are typically used with marine mammals, and these are quite faster than most immobile mistletoe ;) and therefore you could even completely change the game: still have a single observer protocol and set up independent trials to estimate g0. This is akin to say incorporating an independent estimate of g0 for burrowed desert tortoises, or some such. Feel free to contact me on the side if you think this is a potential way to go and you'd like to discuss it further.

Cheers,

T
